name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Tiruvothur
deity: Shiva as Vedapureeswarar, with the goddess Balambikai (Ilamulai Ammai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
summary: Vedapureeswarar is the Shiva temple of Tiruvothur in the Thondai country, a Paadal Petra Sthalam remembered above all for the child-saint Sambandar's miracle, in which a barren male palmyra was made to bear fruit like a female tree.

sections.history: Tiruvothur, called Thiruvothur in the Tevaram hymns, stands in the Thondai country of northern Tamil Nadu near the Cheyyar river. It is among the old living Shiva shrines of the region, praised in the Tevaram by the child-saint Tirugnana Sambandar, which counts it among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the temples sung by the Tamil Shaiva saints. Tradition reads the Lord's name, Vedapureeswarar, as the master of the sacred Vedas. The present stone temple was raised and enlarged by the medieval patrons of the Tamil country and has been kept in worship ever since; the dynasty and date of its first building are not firmly recorded.
sections.architecture: Built in the Dravidian manner, the temple holds the Shiva linga as Vedapureeswarar in its sanctum, while the goddess Balambikai, also called Ilamulai Ammai, is honoured in her own shrine. The temple's sacred tree, its sthala vruksham, is the palmyra palm, and Tiruvothur is counted among the small handful of Shiva temples whose associated tree is the palm. A sculpture set in the inner corridor shows the palm beside the Shiva linga with Sambandar standing near, carved in memory of the miracle for which the shrine is best loved.
sections.legends: The great legend of Tiruvothur is Sambandar's. A devotee who tended the temple grounds had raised palmyra palms there, but grieved that they were all male and would bear no fruit. Moved by his sorrow, the child-saint sang a decad of verses in praise of the Lord of Tiruvothur, and by the grace of Shiva the barren male palms were changed into fruit-bearing female trees. From this the temple keeps the memory of a Lord who makes the barren fruitful, and the palm is honoured as its sacred tree to this day.
sections.festivals: The temple's principal festival is the Brahmotsavam, kept over ten days with street processions, whose seventh-day car festival draws the deities through the town with special grandeur. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Tiruvothur rewards an unhurried visit. Come first to the sanctum of Vedapureeswarar, then turn to the goddess Balambikai in her own shrine, and pause before the carving of the palm and the saint that holds the temple's defining story. The palmyra kept as the sacred tree gives the courtyard its particular character, and devotees who come to pray for fruitfulness and for children hold the place dear. The town sits on the Thondai plain, but within the walls the temple keeps the quiet of a very old sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvothur adjoins Cheyyar town in Tiruvannamalai district, on the road between Kanchipuram and Vandavasi. Cheyyar is served by frequent buses from Kanchipuram, around 40 km away, and from Vellore; the nearest major railheads are at Kanchipuram and Arakkonam, and Chennai is the nearest airport. Confirm distances and connections locally.
